title: What Ireland Gets Right About Reading
author: ReadWriteJen
summary: Ireland has emerged as one of the strongest reading-performing nations in the world -- second in PISA 2022 (516, far above the OECD average of 476) and second in PIRLS 2021 (577) -- prompting international researchers to ask what Ireland is doing right. The author, an Irish literacy educator, pauses to acknowledge this achievement while carefully noting its limits: guided reading, cueing prompts, and leveled texts persist in Irish classrooms, and socioeconomic gaps remain. Jennifer Buckingham's Churchill Fellowship report and a National Center on Education and the Economy (NCEE) case study have both examined Irish literacy instruction for exportable lessons. The article situates Ireland's success within a broader argument that the field spends too much time on problems and not enough examining high-performing systems. By identifying what Ireland does at scale -- elements of structured literacy within a relatively coherent national system -- the author offers a corrective to the relentless deficit framing that dominates international literacy debates.
points: Ireland achieved second place in both PISA 2022 reading (516 vs. OECD average 476) and PIRLS 2021 (577), making it consistently one of the world's strongest reading systems across multiple assessment cycles and age groups.

International researchers including Jennifer Buckingham (Churchill Fellowship) and the NCEE have begun formally studying Irish literacy instruction for lessons applicable to other jurisdictions -- a shift from Ireland receiving advice to Ireland giving it.

The author is careful not to overclaim: problematic practices (guided reading, cueing prompts, leveled texts) persist in Irish classrooms, and achievement gaps remain -- success is real but incomplete.

Ireland's PIRLS 2021 result requires careful interpretation: Irish children were tested at the start of fifth class rather than the end of fourth, due to COVID school closures, so direct international comparisons need adjustment -- though Ireland's elite ranking across multiple cycles is well-established.

The article makes a methodological argument: that literacy improvement conversations fixate on what fails while systematically underexamining what succeeds, and Ireland is an underused case study for the latter.
quotes: Practices such as guided reading, cueing prompts and levelled texts continue to exist in some classrooms despite growing concerns about their effectiveness for beginning and struggling readers. But acknowledging those challenges should not prevent us from recognising success where it exists.

There Is No Secret Formula One of the things I appreciated most about both reports was their refusal to look for a miracle solution. There is no secret Irish reading programme, no single policy that explains our success, no literacy silver bullet.

We Take Teacher Education Seriously Both international reports identified teacher preparation as one of the strengths of the Irish education system. Jennifer Buckingham's Churchill Fellowship report highlights the quality of Irish teacher education and the strong emphasis placed on literacy within programmes preparing future teachers.

We Built Strong Foundations in Early Reading One finding that stood out in both reports was the extent to which systematic phonics is embedded in Irish schools. According to the NCEE report, approximately 95% of classes teach phonics daily, and synthetic phonics programmes have been widely used in primary schools for decades.

One of the things I admire about many Irish classrooms is that they continue to make space for both. Alongside phonics lessons and spelling instruction, you will often find teachers reading novels aloud, discussing picturebooks, sharing poetry and nurturing a love of literature.
We also need to continue improving the quality and consistency of reading instruction. Not all classroom practices align with contemporary evidence.

As a profession, we should continue asking difficult questions about what needs to improve, advocating for children who are not yet being well served, and challenging practices that are not supported by evidence. But every now and then, it is worth pausing to recognise what is working, because understanding success may be just as important as understanding failure.
